explainBack.question: Why does CRISP matching a senior specialist in this study not prove that using CRISP would improve patient care?
explainBack.answer: Because the study only watched normal care: CRISP's predictions were compared against what specialists did, but they were never used to change any surgical decision. Agreement under those observed, time-pressured conditions shows the model can read frozen sections well; it does not show that inserting its predictions into the workflow leads to better decisions or better patient outcomes. That requires an interventional study where CRISP actually influences care and patients are then followed.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P003 (observational study defined as watching normal care), P004 (CRISP predicts, pathologist still decides), P005 (authors say a care-changing, outcome-following study is still needed).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; a careful reader can reconstruct it from P003–P005 without outside knowledge.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A hospital pilots an AI that reads incoming ECGs in the emergency department. In a six-month study, clinicians treated patients as usual while the AI silently flagged heart attacks; its flags matched the senior cardiologist's calls and beat two older algorithms.
unseenTransfer.question: Does this show the hospital should switch to AI-first ECG triage to save lives?
unseenTransfer.answer: No. As with CRISP, the AI only shadowed normal care — its flags never changed who was treated or how fast. Matching the cardiologist under observed conditions shows reading skill, not that acting on the AI's flags would speed correct treatment or avoid new errors. The hospital needs a trial where the flags actually drive triage and patient outcomes are then measured.
